papers.title: NCCN Guidelines® Insights: Colon Cancer, Version 3.2026
papers.journal_full: Journal of the National Comprehensive Cancer Network : JNCCN
papers.authors: Benson A, Venook A, Adam M, Ambelil M, Bray A, Chang G
papers.abstract: Colorectal cancer is the fourth most frequently diagnosed cancer and the second leading cause of cancer death in the United States. Treatment of localized disease usually includes surgery, sometimes followed by adjuvant systemic therapy, while advanced or metastatic disease is often treated with multiple lines of systemic therapy, based on biomarker status. These NCCN Guidelines Insights detail recent updates to the NCCN Guidelines for Colon Cancer, including recommendations for pretreatment DPYD testing to decrease the risk of severe fluoropyrimidine toxicity; updates to adjuvant therapy of nonmetastatic colon cancer based on the results of recent clinical trials; and a reorganization of the systemic therapies for advanced or metastatic disease based on biomarker status, highlighting changes to the treatment recommendations for BRAF V600E mutation-positive disease.

papers.title: Pilot prospective crossover study assessing the role of bile acid malabsorption in the causation and treatment of major low anterior resection syndrome: randomized clinical trial
papers.authors: Woodfield J, Clifford K, Thomas R, Richards S, Fowler A, Alquassab M
papers.abstract:
BACKGROUND: Major low anterior resection syndrome (LARS) affects approximately 60% of rectal cancer survivors, causing urgency and decreased bowel control, reducing quality of life. Bile acid malabsorption (BAM) is an under-recognized contributor whose prevalence and treatment efficacy remain unclear. This proof-of-concept study evaluated the effectiveness of colesevelam for treating LARS and described the prevalence of BAM.
METHODS: This double-blind randomized placebo-controlled crossover trial was conducted between 2021 and 2024 in New Zealand. Adults aged 18-85 years with major LARS received colesevelam (up to 1.25 g, three times daily) or placebo for 5 weeks, separated by a 6-week washout period. A subset of patients underwent 75-selenium homocholic acid taurine (SeHCAT) testing for BAM. The outcomes of interest included changes in the LARS score, Fecal Incontinence Quality of Life Scale (FIQL), and Short-Form 12 (SF-12) questionnaire, with a composite outcome reflecting clinically important improvements.
RESULTS: Of 80 eligible patients, 49 were randomized. However, 36 patients completed the study after washout and were included in a per-protocol analysis (mean age 71 years; 69% male). In these 36 patients, colesevelam did not significantly improve LARS scores, but did significantly improve the SF-12 mental component summary (median +2.36; 95% confidence interval 0.00 to 10.25; P < 0.01) and FIQL depression/self-perception. Eight of 19 patients (42%) had BAM and exhibited significant improvements in SF-12 physical and mental item scores with colesevelam. Using composite criteria, colesevelam produced a 33% response rate, versus 8% for placebo, with higher rates in BAM-positive (50%) than BAM-negative (11%) patients.
CONCLUSIONS: BAM is a treatable contributor to LARS, present in 40% of tested patients. Although treating all LARS patients with bile acid sequestrants provides limited benefit, SeHCAT testing identifies patients likely to respond. BAM assessment would be beneficial if incorporated into LARS management.

papers.title: Robotic versus laparoscopic transanal minimally invasive surgery (TAMIS) for rectal neoplasms: a systematic review, meta-analysis, and IDEAL framework mapping
papers.authors: Prete F, Prete F, De Luca G, Mongardini F, Rasool W, Gupta M
papers.abstract: Transanal minimally invasive surgery(TAMIS) enables local excision of selected rectal neoplasms. Robotic TAMIS(R-TAMIS) may overcome technical constraints of conventional laparoscopic TAMIS(L-TAMIS), but whether these capabilities translate into better outcomes remains uncertain. We compared R-TAMIS and L-TAMIS, examining the evidence in the context of robotic procedural maturity. PubMed, Scopus, and Cochrane Library were searched through 2026 for comparative studies of adults undergoing TAMIS for rectal neoplasm. Risk of bias, certainty of evidence, and procedural maturity were assessed using ROBINS-I, GRADE, and the IDEAL framework. Random-effects meta-analyses were performed. Six retrospective comparative cohorts including 314 patients were identified. R-TAMIS was associated with a higher likelihood of full-thickness resection (OR 11.77, 95%CI 1.40-98.85; P = 0.02), an outcome not appropriate for every lesion. R0 resection was comparable(OR 1.30, 95%CI 0.49-3.47; P = 0.60), with no significant differences in operative time, estimated blood loss, complications, conversion, readmission, or length of stay. Hospital costs tended to be higher with R-TAMIS(I²=99%). All outcomes were supported by very-low-certainty evidence. IDEAL assessment showed that R-TAMIS was introduced in centres with established L-TAMIS experience, while the robotic technique remained in an earlier phase of development. Comparative evidence shows broadly comparable outcomes. Difference in achieved excision depth requires confirmation using standardized outcome definitions and clinically appropriate case selection. These results were achieved despite greater procedural maturity of L-TAMIS and, in some cohorts, more challenging robotic case selection. This developmental asymmetry highlights the need to determine whether maturation and standardization of R-TAMIS will translate its technical capabilities into clinically meaningful advantages in appropriately selected, technically demanding lesions.

papers.title: Prediction models for postoperative anastomotic stricture in rectal cancer: a systematic review
papers.authors: Tan W, Liu L, Tang L, Huang R, Yuan Q, Cai S
papers.abstract:
OBJECTIVE: Systematically evaluate the performance and methodological quality of predictive models for the risk of anastomotic stricture after rectal cancer surgery to provide evidence-based guidance for clinical practice.
METHODS: We comprehensively searched nine Chinese and English databases (CNKI, Wanfang, VIP, Sinomed, PubMed, Web of Science, Cochrane Library, CINAHL, and Embase) for relevant studies published until June 7, 2025. Two independent researchers screened the literature, extracted data, and assessed methodological quality using the Prediction Model Risk of Bias Assessment Tool (PROBAST).
RESULTS: Nine eligible studies were included, demonstrating AUC values ranging from 0.739 to 0.911 in derivation cohorts. Internal validation results were reported in three studies (AUC: 0.905-0.930), while two studies provided test-set validation (AUC:0.818-0.888). The most significant predictors included anastomotic leakage, the use of a protective stoma, and the anastomotic distance. All studies exhibited high risk of bias according to PROBAST criteria, primarily due to retrospective designs, inappropriate handling of continuous variables (dichotomization), inadequate sample sizes, improper management of missing data, univariate-based predictor selection, and insufficient model validation. However, two studies demonstrated good clinical applicability.
CONCLUSION: Research on predictive models for anastomotic stricture after rectal cancer surgery is still in its early stages, constrained by methodological flaws and a lack of external validation that limit their clinical applicability. Future studies should prioritize external validation across diverse populations to confirm their generalizability.

papers.title: Urothelial Carcinoma in Lynch Syndrome: Clinical and Molecular Insights From a Large Multicenter Cohort
papers.authors: Schuler A, Engel C, Ahadova A, van Beekum K, Aretz S, Fechner G
papers.abstract:
PURPOSE: Lynch syndrome (LS), caused by pathogenic germline variants (PGVs) in DNA mismatch repair (MMR) genes, confers increased risks of colorectal, endometrial, and extracolonic malignancies. Urothelial carcinoma (UC) contributes substantially to LS-associated morbidity and mortality. We assessed its frequency, clinical presentation, genotype-associated risk, and molecular features.
METHODS: We retrospectively analyzed genetically confirmed adult LS carriers in the nationwide German Consortium for Familial Intestinal Cancer registry. UC diagnoses identified by International Classification of Diseases, 10th Revision codes C65-C68 underwent manual clinical and pathologic validation. Available tumors underwent centralized pathologic review, MMR immunohistochemistry, and microsatellite instability (MSI) testing.
RESULTS: Among 3,274 LS carriers, 144 (4.4%) had 224 primary UCs. The median age at first UC was 55 years (range, 22-79 years), and UC was the first malignancy in 50 patients (34.7%). Of 202 tumors with known location, 114 (56.4%) arose in the upper urinary tract. Metachronous and synchronous primary UCs occurred in 23 patients (16.0%) and five patients (3.5%), respectively. MSH2-associated PGVs were present in 111 patients (77.1%). In multivariable analysis, MSH2/EPCAM carrier status was associated with UC risk (hazard ratio, 4.43 [95% CI, 2.85 to 6.89]), whereas previous colorectal cancer and UC family history were not. Among 109 patients with diagnostic information, 26 (23.9%) presented with urinary tract-related symptoms, 20 (18.3%) were diagnosed incidentally, and 11 (10.1%) were diagnosed during urologic or oncologic surveillance. Of 31 lesions from 18 patients, 29 (93.6%) were mismatch repair-deficient (dMMR) and 30 (96.8%) were MSI-high; all patients had at least one dMMR tumor and at least one MSI-high tumor.
CONCLUSION: UC in LS occurs relatively early, is strongly associated with MSH2/EPCAM carrier status, and represents the first malignancy in one third of patients. These findings support prospective evaluation of genotype-adapted surveillance.

papers.title: Resident mucosal programmes in colon cancer: organ-associated formation and remodelling of the immune niche
papers.authors: Jiang W, Pan B, Song Z, Zhang Z, Yan H
papers.abstract: Resident epithelial, immune and stromal cells organise immune responses in the colonic mucosa, but their contribution to the immune environment of colon cancer remains incompletely understood. We propose that colonic tumours may partly use pre-existing mucosal cells and regulatory mechanisms, a possibility we refer to as co-option. Chronic colitis provides a comparison for examining changes in mucosal immunity, without implying that inflammation is a necessary precursor to sporadic colon cancer. Colonic BTNL3/BTNL8 proteins regulate resident γδ T-cell subsets, and compartmentalised antigen presentation shapes local immune responses. In mouse models of colitis-associated cancer, resident stromal cells give rise to MCAM+ cancer-associated fibroblasts that promote macrophage recruitment through IL-34/CCL8 signalling. Tumour-associated immune changes include shifts in γδ T-cell subset composition and altered functions of RORγt+ regulatory T cells. MHC class II-dependent interactions between group 3 innate lymphoid cells and T cells also support microbiota-dependent antitumour immunity. Shared signalling is exemplified by the IL-22-oncostatin M-STAT3 pathway in experimental colitis and colitis-associated cancer. However, similarity in cell states and signalling does not establish that tumours preserve pre-existing multicellular mucosal niches. Much of the causal evidence derives from colitis-associated cancer models, and its relevance to sporadic colon cancer remains uncertain. Whether tumours use the same mucosal cells and regulatory mechanisms requires direct testing. Defining tumour-associated changes in these mechanisms may reveal therapeutic targets while preserving protective intestinal immunity.

papers.title: Postoperative Management After Curative-Intent Resection of Colorectal Liver Metastases: A Critical Review of Recent Randomized Evidence
papers.authors: Sagawa T, Hirakawa M, Nagashima H, Fujikawa K
papers.abstract:
BACKGROUND: Postoperative management after curative-intent treatment of colorectal liver metastases (CRLM) remains controversial because improvements in recurrence-related outcomes have not consistently translated into longer overall survival (OS).
METHODS: This critical narrative review examines randomized evidence for systemic chemotherapy and hepatic arterial infusion (HAI), together with emerging evidence on circulating tumor DNA (ctDNA). Trial-based findings, prognostic associations, and unvalidated treatment-effect hypotheses were critically distinguished.
RESULTS: Postoperative fluoropyrimidine- or oxaliplatin-based treatment can delay recurrence in some settings, but a durable OS benefit has not been consistently demonstrated. Contemporary HAI trials differ in patient selection, regional drugs, systemic therapy, and endpoints. PACHA-01 reported improved hepatic recurrence-free survival in a selected population, HARVEST was terminated early, and PUMP did not meet its primary endpoint. These findings neither establish routine HAI nor identify validated predictors of benefit. Postoperative ctDNA is strongly prognostic, but nonrandomized associations between adjuvant treatment and outcomes cannot establish the clinical utility of ctDNA-directed treatment allocation.
CONCLUSIONS: A conceptual distinction between hepatic and systemic recurrence risk may support multidisciplinary deliberation and prospective trial design, but should not be used as a validated postoperative treatment-selection algorithm. Clinical decisions must also account for prior chemotherapy, postoperative recovery, toxicity, local treatment opportunities, institutional expertise, and patient preferences.
